title: The Book Machine
subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own
throughline: Follow one GitHub issue as it travels through CI, gets built into a narrated explainer, and lands on the shelf — then learn to run the whole loop yourself.

chapters.title: A shelf that builds itself
chapters.blurb: The whole loop at a glance: an issue goes in, a published explainer comes out.

story.title: A shelf that builds itself
story.subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own

steps.title: The Book Machine
steps.narration: This repo is a **library of generated explainers**. You don't edit files to add one — you open an issue, and the machine builds and publishes it.
steps.say: This whole repository is a library of generated explainers. To add a new one, you don't edit any files. You open an issue, and the machine builds it and publishes it for you.
steps.coverSubtitle: One issue in, one published explainer out

steps.title: You are the curator
steps.narration: Your only job is to decide *what* to explain. No storyboards, no audio editing, no deploys by hand.
steps.say: Your only job is to decide what to explain. There are no storyboards to write by hand, no audio to edit, and no deploys to run yourself.

steps.title: An issue is the trigger
steps.narration: You open one of two issue templates — `new-book` or `new-series` — and fill in a short form.
steps.say: You open one of two issue templates, new book or new series, and fill in a short form describing what you want.

steps.title: CI picks it up
steps.narration: Opening the issue fires the `new-book.yml` workflow in **GitHub Actions** — the engine room.
steps.say: Opening that issue fires the new book workflow in GitHub Actions. That is the engine room where everything happens.

steps.title: The generator builds it
steps.narration: CI runs the **generator**: it digests the source, narrates it, draws an O'RLY cover, and adds icons.
steps.say: Inside CI, the generator does the work. It digests the source, narrates the script, draws a parody cover, and adds icons to the diagram.

steps.title: It deploys to Pages
steps.narration: The finished book is committed, merged, and **deployed to GitHub Pages** — no button to press.
steps.say: The finished book is committed, merged, and deployed to GitHub Pages automatically. There is no button for you to press.

steps.title: The loop closes
steps.narration: The new book appears on your **shelf** — and you're ready to open the next issue. That's the whole loop.
steps.say: The new book appears on your shelf, and you are ready to open the next issue. That is the entire loop, and the rest of this book opens up each step.

chapters.title: Open an issue, pull the trigger
chapters.blurb: Two issue templates, one guarded workflow — and why only your issues run it.

story.title: Open an issue, pull the trigger
story.subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own

steps.title: Open an issue, pull the trigger
steps.narration: Adding a book starts with an **issue form** — and a guard makes sure only *your* issues can spend real money on generation.
steps.say: Adding a book starts with an issue form. And a guard makes sure only your own issues can ever spend real money on generation.

steps.title: Two issue forms
steps.narration: `new-book.yml` asks for a repo + subsystem; `new-series.yml` asks for a source + the books in the series. Structured fields, not free text.
steps.say: There are two forms. New book asks for a repo and a subsystem. New series asks for a source and the books you want in the series. They use structured fields, not free text.

steps.title: Each form sets a label
steps.narration: Every template auto-applies a **label** at creation — `new-book` or `new-series` — which is how the workflow tells the two apart.
steps.say: Every template automatically applies a label when the issue is created, either new book or new series. That label is how the workflow tells the two apart.

steps.title: The workflow listens
steps.narration: `new-book.yml` runs `on: issues: opened` — so creating *any* issue wakes the workflow up.
steps.say: The new book workflow listens on the issues opened event. So creating any issue at all wakes the workflow up.

steps.title: The guard checks two things
steps.narration: An `if:` gate runs the job only when the issue author **is the repo owner** *and* carries a book/series label. Random visitors can't trigger billable work.
steps.say: But an if condition guards the job. It runs only when the issue author is the repository owner, and the issue carries a book or series label. Random visitors simply cannot trigger billable work.

steps.title: Only then, the job runs
steps.narration: If both checks pass, the **generate job** spins up on a fresh Ubuntu runner and the real work begins.
steps.say: If both checks pass, the generate job spins up on a fresh Ubuntu runner, and the real work finally begins.

steps.title: A form, a label, a guard
steps.narration: So: a structured **form**, an automatic **label**, and an owner-only **guard**. The next chapter is what the job actually does.
steps.say: So it is a structured form, an automatic label, and an owner only guard. The next chapter is what that job actually does once it starts.

chapters.title: Claude Code runs the pipeline
chapters.blurb: Inside the job: Claude follows a playbook and runs the generator end to end.

story.title: Claude Code runs the pipeline
story.subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own

steps.title: Claude Code runs the pipeline
steps.narration: The job hands the issue to **Claude Code**, which follows a playbook and drives the whole generator.
steps.say: The job hands the issue to Claude Code, running headless in the action. Claude follows a playbook and drives the whole generator from start to finish.

steps.title: Claude Code, headless
steps.narration: `claude-code-action@v1` runs with the issue's title and body as its prompt, authenticated by your subscription token.
steps.say: The claude code action, version one, runs with the issue title and body as its prompt. It is authenticated by your Claude subscription token.

steps.title: It follows a playbook
steps.narration: Claude reads `.claude/commands/new-book.md` or `new-series.md` — the same step-by-step recipe a human would follow.
steps.say: Claude reads the matching playbook, either new book or new series, in the dot claude commands folder. It is the same step by step recipe a human would follow.

steps.title: The orchestrator
steps.narration: The playbook digests the source and writes a storyboard, then runs `generator/cli.mjs` — the orchestrator that calls every stage.
steps.say: The playbook digests the source and writes a storyboard, then runs the command line orchestrator, cli dot m j s, which calls every stage in turn.

steps.title: Keys come from secrets
steps.narration: The OpenAI, ElevenLabs, and Noun Project keys arrive as **repo secrets** in the environment — never committed, never printed.
steps.say: The open A I, eleven labs, and noun project keys arrive as repository secrets, passed into the environment. They are never committed to the repo and never printed.

steps.title: Narrate with exact cues
steps.narration: `tts.mjs` sends each step's text to **ElevenLabs** and reads back per-character timestamps, so slides land exactly on the words.
steps.say: The text to speech stage sends each step's script to eleven labs, and reads back per character timestamps. That is how the slides land exactly on the spoken words.

steps.title: Cover and icons
steps.narration: `cover.mjs` makes the O'RLY animal with **gpt-image** (a QA loop rejects stray text), and the **Noun Project** icons land on every node.
steps.say: The cover stage draws the parody animal with g p t image, and a quality loop rejects any stray text. Then noun project icons are placed on every node of the diagram.

steps.title: Out comes a book
steps.narration: The result: a `public/generated/<slug>/` folder plus an updated `library.json` — a complete, self-contained book.
steps.say: The result is a generated folder for the new slug, plus an updated library file. That is a complete, self contained book, ready to publish.

chapters.title: Pull request, auto-merge, redeploy
chapters.blurb: How the built book reaches the live shelf — and why it needs your PAT.

story.title: Pull request, auto-merge, redeploy
story.subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own

steps.title: Pull request, auto-merge, redeploy
steps.narration: The book is built — now it has to reach the live site. The workflow opens a PR, merges it, and lets the deploy fire.
steps.say: The book is built, but now it has to reach the live site. The workflow opens a pull request, merges it, and lets the deploy fire on its own.
steps.coverSubtitle: Why the loop needs your PAT

steps.title: Commit to a branch
steps.narration: The job creates `book/issue-N` and commits everything under `public/generated` to it.
steps.say: The job creates a branch named for the issue, and commits everything under the generated folder onto it.

steps.title: Open a pull request
steps.narration: `gh pr create` opens a PR whose body says **`Closes #N`**, so merging it will close the original issue.
steps.say: The g h command line opens a pull request whose body says closes, and the issue number. So merging it will automatically close the original issue.

steps.title: Merge it automatically
steps.narration: `gh pr merge --squash --admin` merges immediately — no human review needed for your own collection.
steps.say: Then the merge command, with squash and admin, merges it immediately. No human review is needed for your own collection.

steps.title: Why a PAT, not the default token
steps.narration: Crucial detail: a merge made with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` would **not** re-trigger other workflows. Using your **`GH_PAT`** does, so the deploy can run.
steps.say: Here is the crucial detail. A merge made with the built in github token would not re trigger any other workflow. Using your personal access token does, which is the only reason the deploy can run next.

steps.title: The deploy fires
steps.narration: Because a PAT pushed to `main`, `deploy.yml` runs: a `PAGES=1` Vite build with base `/orly/`, uploaded as a Pages artifact.
steps.say: Because the token pushed to main, the deploy workflow runs. It does a pages build with Vite, using the orly base path, and uploads the result as a pages artifact.

steps.title: The shelf updates
steps.narration: Pages publishes the new artifact, the issue closes itself, and within a minute the book is **live** on the shelf.
steps.say: Pages publishes the new artifact, the issue closes itself, and within about a minute the new book is live on the shelf for everyone to read.

chapters.title: Fork it, set your env, make your own
chapters.blurb: Five minutes of setup and the same self-building loop is yours.

story.title: Fork it, set your env, make your own
story.subtitle: From a GitHub issue to a published explainer — fork your own

steps.title: Fork it, set your env, make your own
steps.narration: Everything you just saw runs from config in *this* repo. Fork it, add your keys, and the same machine builds **your** collection.
steps.say: Everything you just saw runs from configuration inside this very repo. Fork it, add your own keys, and the exact same machine builds your collection instead of mine.
steps.coverSubtitle: Five minutes of setup and the loop is yours

steps.title: Fork the repo
steps.narration: Click **Fork**. You get the whole pipeline — the generator, the workflows, the shelf — in your own account.
steps.say: First, click fork. You get the entire pipeline: the generator, the workflows, and the shelf, all in your own account.

steps.title: Set your env vars
steps.narration: Add the repo secrets the workflow expects: `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `GH_PAT`, and your `OPENAI`, `ELEVENLABS`, and `NOUN_PROJECT` keys.
steps.say: Next, add the repository secrets the workflow expects. Your Claude code token, your personal access token, and your open A I, eleven labs, and noun project keys.

steps.title: Enable Pages
steps.narration: Turn on **GitHub Pages** with the *Actions* source. The build already targets the `/orly/` base path in `vite.config.ts`.
steps.say: Then enable GitHub Pages, using the actions source. The build already targets the orly base path, set in the vite config.

steps.title: Open your first issue
steps.narration: Now open a `new-book` or `new-series` issue on **your** fork. The guard sees *you* as the owner, so it runs.
steps.say: Now open a new book or new series issue on your own fork. The guard sees you as the owner this time, so it runs for you.

steps.title: Your collection, self-building
steps.narration: Minutes later it lands at **`you.github.io/orly`**. Open another issue any time — your shelf grows itself.
steps.say: Minutes later, your first explainer lands at your own github pages site. Open another issue any time you like, and your shelf simply grows itself.

steps.title: The machine is yours
steps.narration: Fork, secrets, Pages, issue. From here on, *describing* a book is the only work — the **Book Machine** does the rest.
steps.say: Fork, secrets, pages, issue. From here on, describing a book is the only work you ever do. The book machine does all the rest.
